newsitem.title: UK: EU farm policy reform inevitable, Agra Europe told.
newsitem.headline: EU farm policy reform inevitable, Agra Europe told.

text.p: Deep rooted reform of the EU's Common Agricultural Policy is inevitable, according to one of the CAP's long standing critics, Brussels based expert Brian Gardner.
"I don't have to advocate it. All I have to do is point out that it is inevitable," Gardner told the Agra Europe Outlook conference in London on Thursday.

Much of the pressure for reform would come from the budget. "Agriculture policy continues to occupy too big a share of the union budget," Gardner said, although he accepted that ministers would always find the money to do what they want to.
However, he now believed that the upward trend in EU farm spending was not acceptable to politicians.

"I see some attempt to reduce spending in the area most in need of pruning, which is of course the cereals sector," he said. "One of the anomalies in the post reform period," he said, referring to the previous, 1992, reform of the CAP, "is the huge share of subsidies taken by the cereals sector."
The huge pre-reform cost of export subsidies had been replaced by the cost of arable area payments, the so-called compensation element of the 1992 reform.

Gardner expected to see compensatory payments come under pressure, notably from the Cairns group of agricultural exporting countries, in the next round of world trade talks. "We quite clearly have to got rid of compensatory payements, "Gardner said.

He was sceptical about how fast the EU would reform its farm policy, but he expected it to happen eventually. "Sooner or later the pressures I have talked about will force radical reform to take place," he said.
The system in its current form was defended by Dr Dterd Goeman, the director of policy and market affairs at the German food ministry.
He saw no point in reforming the CAP ahead of the trade talks.

"The EU's negotiatiing position would be weakened substantially by the initiation of considerable systematic changes within the EU, as the EU's partners will then demand further concessions," he said.
European monetary union would require no major changes in the CAP, he felt.
